newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain condemns world neglect of central Africa.
newsitem.headline: Spain condemns world neglect of central Africa.

text.p: Spain condemned the international community on Thursday for neglecting dire problems in central Africa for years and also criticised regional leaders such as South African President Nelson Mandela.

Spain has lined up behind France to press for a multinational military force which would open humanitarian corridors to aid 1.2 million starving refugees in eastern Zaire, a proposal which has been greeted coolly by other nations.
"(There has been) great carelessness by the world community," Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said.
Since violence erupted between Rwanda and Burundi in 1994, he said the international community had only addressed the symptons, not the causes of the conflict.

The Spanish minister said this had happened "without credible regional leaders like Mandela thinking of setting up an African multinational force" with the aim of formulating a policy of conflict prevention.

A Zairean envoy to South Africa said on Thursday Mandela had promised to play a major diplomatic role in ending the fighting between Zaire's army and ethnic Tutsi rebels backed by Rwanda. But it was not clear what he would do to help bring peace to the Great Lakes region.
Spain's condemnation echoed a harsh indictment of world inaction by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on Wednesday.
"The main obstacle is the international community's spinelessness," de Charette said of efforts to aid the refugees.

Matutes endorsed a multinational force which would also include African soldiers. He said a neutral force should be dispatched whose mission would be "not to impose peace but to prevent a catastrophe".

A foreign ministry spokesman in Madrid said on Wednesday Spain and France wanted to send a force of at least 5,000 soldiers to Zaire but would not go ahead with any plan unless the United States and the United Nations backed it.
A minimum of 5,000 soldiers would be needed to open humanitarian corridors and facilitate the distribution of food, water and medicine to the refugees, he added.

France would send about 1,000 troops, Spain has pledged somewhat less, and the two countries hoped the United States and other nations would contribute thousands more. But the only other country promising to commit troops so far is Ethiopia.
The spokesman said the plan envisages a three-phased approach under which the multinational force would gradually be replaced by African troops.

While politicians in Europe and the United States mulled the complexities of mounting an aid operation to the war zone, there were eyewitness reports that Rwandan refugees were dying of thirst in a mountainous region of east Zaire.

European Union aid ministers met in Brussels on Thursday to try to define a joint approach to the deepening tragedy. The crisis will also be on the agenda of a British-French summit beginning in Bordeaux, France on Thursday.
